ety.text: Borrowed from French fédération, from Late Latin foederatio, from Latin foederare; equivalent to federate + -ion.

senses.d: An act of joining together into a single political entity.
An array of nations or states that are unified under one central authority.
Any society or organisation formed from separate groups or bodies.
ex: FIDE appeals to all chess players and federations to accept this view.

senses.d: A collection of network or telecommunication providers that offer interoperability.
Of an architectural style popular around the time of federation.
ex: We live in a federation house.
The Federation house claimed a unique place in architecture, even if it offended architects.

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin foederātiōnem. By surface analysis, fédérer + -ation.

ety.text: From Late Latin foederātiōnem (“federation, treaty”), derived from Latin foederō (“to sign a treaty or agreement”), derived from foedus (“pact, agreement”).
Borrowed from Late Latin foederātiōnem. Analyzable as federar + -ción.
Learned borrowing from Latin foederātiōnem. By surface analysis, federar + -ção.

phr: Federation of Saint Christopher and Nevis

ety.text: Latin -ālisbor. Old French -al Middle French -al French -al French fédéralbor. English federal Borrowed from French fédéral, from Latin foedus + French -al.

senses.d: Pertaining to a league or treaty; derived from an agreement or covenant between parties, especially between nations.
Pertaining to the national government level in a federal nation, as opposed to state, provincial, county, city, or town.
A federal agent or (chiefly law-enforcement) official.
A law-enforcement official of the FBI.
A Union soldier in the American Civil War.
